title: Generative Models: Representation Learning Meets Generative Modeling

sentences.text: We're going to continue on today and this week with generative models.
So today will be on variational autoencoders.
And we're going to give a perspective that generative modeling and representation learning are very tightly coupled.
If you can solve the generative modeling problem, it should help you solve the representation learning problem and vice versa.
And variational autoencoders are going to be one model that really puts the two ideas together and solves them both at the same time.

And this lecture is a little bit different than some of the last few, in that rather than covering a lot of different topics in some superficial level of detail, we're going to just go deep on VAEs, on variational autoencoders.

It might be stochastic, so it's more like a stochastic inverse, but they kind of operate in opposite directions.

roadmap.lecture_goal: understand the theoretical foundations and practical mechanisms of Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) as a bridge between representation learning and generative modeling.

objectives.text: You'll be able to compare representation learning and generative modeling as inverse processes, and identify the limitations of using autoencoder decoders for generative sampling.
You'll be able to define latent variable models, explain the mathematical structure of Mixture of Gaussians (MoG), and describe the framework for sampling from these models.

You'll be able to explain the computational challenges of likelihood maximization and apply Monte Carlo methods, including the reparameterization trick and importance sampling, to approximate marginal likelihoods.
You'll be able to derive and explain the components of the Variational Autoencoder (VAE) objective function, including the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO).
You'll be able to analyze how the tension between compression and reconstruction shapes the VAE latent space, and explain how VAEs learn structured and disentangled representations.

segments.subgoal: Compare representation learning and generative modeling as inverse processes

key_points.text: Representation learning transforms raw data into a structured, abstracted representation, while generative modeling transforms abstract representations back into data.
Generative models are viewed as transformations from a simple prior distribution (noise $z$) to a complicated data distribution ($x$).
The process involves an encoder ($f$) that maps data to latent representations ($z$) and a generator ($g$) that maps latent representations to data.

key_terms.definition: Generative models are transformations that map a simple prior distribution, such as noise, to a complicated data distribution.

Representation learning is the process of transforming raw data into a nicer, structured, and abstracted representation. This process maps data from its original form into a more manageable, abstract space.

The prior distribution is a simple structure distribution, typically representing noise, which is used as the starting point for the generative process. This distribution is mapped to the complicated data distribution.

The encoder is a mapping function, denoted as f, that takes data as input and transforms it into a representation in the latent space. This function is central to the representation learning direction.

segments.subgoal: Identify the limitations of using autoencoder decoders for generative sampling

key_points.text: The decoder part of an autoencoder functions similarly to a generative model, mapping a latent vector z back to data X.
A major difficulty in using an autoencoder for sampling new data is that the distribution of the latent space (z) is unknown.
The latent space learned by an autoencoder may not form a simple distribution that is easy to sample from.
The goal of a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) is to ensure the latent space forms a simple distribution that can be sampled from.

key_terms.definition: Autoencoder is a model that maps input data to a low-dimensional vector space, and then decodes that vector back into the original data for reconstruction.
Decoder is the second half of the autoencoder, which functions as a mapping from a latent vector to the data space.
Generative model is a model that maps a vector to data, allowing it to be used as a generator to sample new random data points.
Variational autoencoder is a type of autoencoder designed to ensure that the latent space forms a simple distribution that can be sampled from.
Latent space is the set of encodings of an autoencoder that the Variational Autoencoder aims to structure into a simple distribution.

segments.subgoal: Define VAEs and explain the function of the Gaussian latent space

key_points.text: A Variational Autoencoder (VAE) is an autoencoder that maps input data to a simple Gaussian distribution in the latent space.
Mapping to a Gaussian allows for generative modeling by sampling from the Gaussian and passing the vectors through the decoder.
VAEs are effective at both representation learning and generative modeling.
Mathematically, VAEs serve as a framework that encompasses many other generative models, including diffusion models.

key_terms.definition: Autoencoder is a model where the encoder maps the input data to a complicated shape, a key difference from a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) which maps to a simple Gaussian.

Gaussian is a simple distribution that the encoder in a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) maps to, contrasting with the complicated shapes that other autoencoders might use. This simple distribution is crucial because it allows the model to sample random vectors from it to generate new data.

segments.subgoal: Define and understand the mathematical structure of Mixture of Gaussians (MoG)

key_points.text: Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) are fundamentally modeled as a mixture of Gaussians (MoG).
A Mixture of Gaussians models complicated distributions by summing multiple individual Gaussian distributions.
A single Gaussian is a density model where parameters (mean and variance) are optimized using a maximum likelihood objective.
The parameters defining a Mixture of Gaussians include the mixing weights (w), the means (mu), and the covariances (sigma) of all components.

key_terms.definition: Mixture of Gaussians is a statistical model used to approximate complicated data distributions that do not have a simple Gaussian shape. This model achieves approximation by summing up multiple individual Gaussian distributions, each weighted by a specific mixing weight.

A Gaussian is a density model fitted to data using a maximum likelihood objective, which attempts to increase the density applied to where the data resides. The parameters that characterize a Gaussian are its mean and its variance.

segments.subgoal: Explain how a finite neural network can parameterize an infinite mixture of Gaussians

key_points.text: Explicitly parameterizing an infinite mixture of Gaussians requires an infinite number of parameters (141-142).
An infinite mixture can be parameterized using a finite set of parameters by mapping from a continuous base distribution via a function g (143-144).
The function g, which is a neural network, takes a sample z and outputs the mean and covariance of a Gaussian component (153-156).
Because the component space is continuous, the total probability density function is found by integrating over the base distribution z (165-170).

key_terms.definition: Mixture of Gaussians is a classical statistical model that combines multiple Gaussian distributions. This model is used to represent complex data distributions by summing several simpler Gaussian components.

Infinite mixture of Gaussians is a model where the components are continuous and infinite, parameterized by a finite set of parameters. This allows the model to fit complex distributions without requiring an explicit, infinite parameterization.

Prior distribution (pz) is the initial distribution from which a random vector is sampled in the latent space. This distribution defines the base continuous space from which the infinite mixture components are generated.

segments.subgoal: Explain the mathematical framework and sampling procedure of latent variable models

key_points.text: The data modeling problem involves fitting a distribution over observed data (x) that is represented as a mapping from an unobserved latent variable (z).
To model the likelihood of a data point x, one must integrate (marginalize) over the unobserved latent variables z.
The goal of fitting a latent variable model is maximizing the marginal likelihood that the model assigns to the data.
A latent variable model provides both a density function for the data and an easy way to sample from that density.
To sample data x, one first samples a latent variable z (e.g., a unit Gaussian) and then decodes it through the generator g.

key_terms.definition: Likelihood is the probability that the model places on the data, which is a measure used when attempting to fit a probability model to observed data. The goal of max likelihood learning is to find the probability model that maximizes this likelihood.
Marginal likelihood is the probability of the data obtained by integrating over all unobserved latent variables. This concept is crucial for fitting a latent variable model to data.

Latent variable model is a statistical framework that represents observed data using underlying, unobserved latent variables. The model is fitted to data by maximizing the marginal likelihood, which requires integrating over all possible settings of those latent variables.

Variational autoencoder is an approach for fitting a latent variable model to data by maximizing the marginal likelihood that the model assigns to the data. This method utilizes an infinite Gaussian mixture model to define the objective function and hypothesis space for learning.
The generator is a conditional distribution, representing the probability over the data given a specific setting of the latent variables. It maps the underlying latent variables to the data space.

segments.subgoal: Explain the computational difficulty of likelihood maximization and the role of the reparameterization trick

key_points.text: Maximizing the likelihood of data requires computing an integral that is computationally intractable and expensive to calculate directly.
The reparameterization trick simplifies sampling from a distribution by transforming a unit Gaussian noise.
The primary challenge in Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) is calculating the data likelihood integral in an efficient manner.
VAEs model the data likelihood by fitting an infinite mixture of Gaussians to the data.

key_terms.definition: Intractable integral is an integral that is difficult to calculate because there is no closed form solution for it. This difficulty prevents direct computation of the likelihood.
Likelihood is the measure of how well a model assigns probability to the observed data. Maximizing the likelihood means perturbing parameters to increase the probability assigned to the data.

segments.subgoal: Apply Monte Carlo methods to approximate the marginal likelihood integral

key_points.text: The objective function for training is the data log likelihood, which requires calculating the marginal likelihood $p_x$ (the probability of the data $x$).
The marginal likelihood integral can be expressed as an expectation over random samples drawn from the prior distribution $p_z$.
Expectations can be approximated using Monte Carlo estimation by taking a finite set of samples and averaging the results.
The approximation involves sampling from the prior $p_z$ (e.g., unit Gaussian) and averaging the likelihood density $p(x|z)$ placed on the data by the model for each sample.

key_terms.definition: Objective function is the mathematical function, denoted L, that the model attempts to maximize during training. This function represents the data log likelihood, which measures how well the model fits the observed data.

Marginal likelihood is the probability of the observed data, $p(x)$, which is calculated by integrating the joint probability of the data and the latent variable over all possible values of the latent variable, $z$.
Log likelihood is the natural logarithm of the marginal likelihood, $p(x)$, and it is used as the primary metric to maximize the model's fit to the data.

Expectation is a mathematical concept that represents the average value of a function over a probability distribution. In this context, the marginal likelihood is equal to the expectation of the likelihood density over random samples from the prior distribution.

Monte Carlo estimate is a method used to approximate an expectation by taking a finite set of samples and calculating their average. As the number of samples increases, this estimate becomes an unbiased estimator of the true integral.

segments.subgoal: Analyze how sample size affects approximation error in high-dimensional spaces

key_points.text: The variance of a Monte Carlo estimator scales as 1 over the square root of the number of samples (M).
Nominally, the Monte Carlo estimator variance does not depend on the dimensionality D.
Intuition suggests that covering a D-dimensional space requires an exponentially increasing number of samples.
In practice, high-dimensional integration requires exponentially more samples to achieve a good approximation.

key_terms.definition: Normal distribution is a probability distribution defined by a mean and a variance, and it has a closed-form analytical form for its density. This density function is expressed using an exponential function involving the difference between the variable and the mean, scaled by the variance.

Monte Carlo estimator is a method used in the approximation step to estimate integrals by drawing samples. The variance of this estimator is inversely proportional to the number of samples used, specifically $1/M$.

Exponential samples refers to the intuition that covering a D-dimensional space requires a number of samples that grows exponentially with the dimension, suggesting that the required sample size depends exponentially on the dimension for a quality fit.

segments.subgoal: Explain how importance sampling improves Monte Carlo estimation for likelihood calculation

key_points.text: Naive Monte Carlo sampling is inefficient because most random samples of z will place nearly zero probability on the target data point x.
Importance sampling approximates an expectation by multiplying by a density q(z) and sampling from q(z) instead of the original density p(z).
The core idea of importance sampling is to sample from a distribution that gives more importance to the points that contribute highly to the likelihood of the data.
The optimal distribution to sample from for estimating the expectation is the conditional density p(z|x).

key_terms.definition: Importance sampling is a technique that approximates an integral by sampling from a distribution $q(z)$ that places higher density on the points that contribute significantly to the integral. This targeted sampling approach is designed to require far fewer samples than naive random sampling from the original distribution $p(z)$, where most samples would yield negligible contributions.

Monte Carlo approximation is a technique that estimates an expectation by randomly sampling variables. Naive Monte Carlo approximation, which involves taking random samples from the prior distribution, is inefficient because most samples may place nearly zero probability on the target data point.

Likelihood is the probability that a generative model places on a specific data point $x$. Estimating this likelihood requires calculating a complex expectation over the latent variable $z$, a process that is often computationally challenging because most random samples contribute negligible probability to the final estimate.
Expectation is the average value of a random variable, which is calculated by integrating over a distribution. In this context, the expectation represents the true likelihood of the data point $x$.

segments.subgoal: Define the encoder and derive the objective function for the VAE

key_points.text: The primary challenge is modeling the distribution of latent variables given the input data, $p(Z|X)$.
The encoder function, $q$, maps the input data $X$ to a distribution over the latent space $Z$ to approximate $p(Z|X)$.
The encoder's objective ($J_q$) is to minimize the KL divergence between the true distribution $p(Z|X)$ and the approximated distribution $q(Z|X)$.
The overall generative model objective ($J_p$) maximizes the likelihood of the data using importance sampling based on the learned distribution $q$.

key_terms.definition: Decoder function is the probability model that defines the probability of the data X given the latent variable Z. This function is one of the two pieces used to construct the full generative model.

Generative model is a model parameterized by a neural network G that places a Gaussian probability over the data space X. This model defines the probability by taking an integral over all possible points in the latent space Z.

segments.subgoal: Explain the derivation and purpose of the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO)

key_points.text: A Monte Carlo estimate of the log of expectation is a biased estimator, which is undesirable for convergence.
By pulling the log inside the expectation, an unbiased estimator of the expectation can be created.
This transformation is mathematically allowed by Jensen's inequality.
The resulting lower bound on the objective function is called the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO).
The ELBO serves as a lower bound to the likelihood of the data under the model, which is the quantity of interest.

key_terms.definition: The Evidence lower bound (ELBO) is a lower bound to the likelihood of the data under the model. This bound is derived using Jensen's inequality.

segments.subgoal: Explain the components and function of the Variational Autoencoder (VAE) objective

key_points.text: The VAE objective is designed to maximize the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) to approximate the likelihood of the data (570, 572).
A VAE resembles an autoencoder but includes a necessary sampling step (adding noise) in the latent space (603, 604).
The VAE objective consists of two terms: a reconstruction error (likelihood) and a KL divergence term (regularization) (606, 625).
The KL divergence term forces the latent distribution to be close to the prior, which prevents the latent space from becoming arbitrarily complex (626, 652).

key_terms.definition: Evidence lower bound is the objective function that the Variational Autoencoder (VAE) maximizes to approximate the likelihood of the data. Maximizing this lower bound allows for joint optimization of the encoder and decoder parameters.

Reconstruction error is the first term of the ELBO, which measures how different the decoded point is from the original input observation $x$. This term essentially quantifies the likelihood of the data given the latent representation.

segments.subgoal: Explain how the tension between compression and reconstruction shapes the VAE latent space

key_points.text: The fundamental tension in a VAE is balancing the drive to compress the latent space toward zero with the need to preserve information for accurate reconstruction.
If Gaussian components in the latent space overlap, it creates ambiguity, meaning two different data points map to the same location, making reconstruction impossible.
The tension between compression and reconstruction forces the latent components to spread out and evenly tile the unit Gaussian distribution.
The Variational Autoencoder (VAE) can be understood as an autoencoder that utilizes approximation and importance sampling techniques.

key_terms.definition: The Fundamental tension is the conflict between two requirements: pushing the latent space towards zero to create a compact shape, and preserving enough information to reconstruct the input data.

Ambiguity occurs when two different data points map to the same point or to overlapping Gaussian components in the latent space. This prevents the model from knowing which input point generated a specific latent representation, thus hindering reconstruction.
The Infinite mixture of Gaussians is a density model used to represent the data distribution. The VAE approximates this continuous distribution using a finite set of samples.

Reconstruction is the process where the model attempts to reproduce the original input point from its compressed latent representation. This process requires the model to preserve sufficient information during compression.

segments.subgoal: Explain the procedure, technical mechanisms, and intuition behind Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)

key_points.text: Optimizing a VAE involves encoding data, adding noise, decoding, and computing losses consisting of squared error and the KL term.
The reparameterization trick is necessary to allow backpropagation through sampling by only optimizing the mean and variance.
The KL divergence penalty encourages the latent space to be dense and smooth, ensuring that every point maps to a valid data point and preventing gaps.
While modeling variance is possible, simpler VAE implementations can often suffice by just adding noise or using a KL penalty.

segments.subgoal: Analyze how VAEs learn disentangled representations from data

key_points.text: VAEs can learn different latent dimensions that control independent factors of variation, a property called disentanglement.
If the data generation process includes underlying parameters (like a normal distribution for grass color), the VAE can recover that true causal factor.
VAEs can also learn abstracted factors of variation (like river curvature) that do not correspond to the original causal mechanisms used to generate the data.
Disentanglement implies independence between the effects of different factors, but these factors do not necessarily map to the original causal mechanisms.

key_terms.definition: Representation learner is a model component, such as an encoder, that is assessed for its independent utility beyond the primary task of generation. Representation learners are useful when the latent space they produce allows for meaningful, controllable variations in the output data.
A latent variable is a variable in the latent space that the model learns to represent the data. These variables are used to control different types of visual variation in the output data.

A disentangled representation is a latent space where different dimensions control independent factors of variation in the data. This means varying one factor, such as color, does not affect another factor, such as curvature.

segments.subgoal: Explain the role of latent variables in achieving structured representations in generative models

key_points.text: Generative models, including GANs, can learn organized latent spaces that serve as good representations of the world, even if they lack an explicit encoder.
All generative models utilize latent or intermediate variables (such as noise or network activations) to learn structured representations of the data.
The process of generative modeling forces the model to learn factors that parsimoniously explain the data and the world.
When mapping complex input topology onto a simple latent space, the resulting map can be smooth but may contain 'seams' or sudden jumps.
Different generative models (VAE, GAN, Diffusion, Autoregressive) possess unique trade-offs regarding latent variables, density functions, and sampling efficiency.

key_terms.definition: Generative modeling is the process that forces a model to explain the world by capturing underlying factors of the data. This explanation can involve capturing independent components or abstract concepts.
Latent variable is a hidden variable that models the structure of the data in generative models. These variables can be sampled to show how the model represents the world.

Disentangled space is a representation where the data is mapped such that different dimensions correspond to independent factors of the input. This allows specific directions in the space to control specific properties of the generated data.
Activation space is the set of values produced by a network's internal layers as it processes data. Directions within this space can be examined to find structured representations of the input data.
Structured representation is a learned feature set that allows a model to fit to the world effectively. This representation must capture factors that can parsimoniously explain the data.

open_questions.prompt: Explain how the Variational Autoencoder (VAE) uses its two objective terms to function as both a reconstruction model and a good representation learner.
open_questions.reference_answer: The VAE objective consists of two main terms: a reconstruction error and a KL divergence term. The first term, which is the likelihood, measures how different the decoded point is from the input observation, functioning similarly to an autoencoder. The second term, the KL divergence, forces the distribution of encodings to be close to a unit Gaussian prior. This KL term is essential because it prevents the latent space from becoming arbitrarily complicated or simply mirroring the raw data. By balancing these two objectives, the VAE ensures that the data is reconstructed accurately while maintaining a structured, compressed latent representation near the origin.

open_questions.prompt: Your friend missed the lecture on Generative Models. Explain the fundamental modeling strategy used in latent variable models, like VAEs, to generate data when the underlying variables are unobserved.
open_questions.reference_answer: Latent variable models, like VAEs, aim to model the data distribution $P(x)$ by mapping from an unobserved latent variable $z$. Since $z$ is unobserved, the model must calculate the likelihood $P(x)$ by marginalizing over $z$. The primary learning goal is to maximize this marginal likelihood, which means finding the probability model $P_\theta$ that assigns the most density to the data. The hypothesis space for this model is often defined as an infinite mixture of Gaussians. Finally, sampling is achieved by first sampling a unit Gaussian $z$ and then decoding it through the generator $g$.

open_questions.prompt: Explain how the lecture segment addresses the challenge of calculating the integral in the marginal likelihood when training generative models.
open_questions.reference_answer: The marginal likelihood involves an integral over latent variables, which is difficult to compute directly. However, this integral can be re-expressed as an expectation over random samples from the prior $p_z$. To approximate this expectation, we use a Monte Carlo estimate by taking a finite set of samples and averaging the likelihood density. This process replaces the continuous integral with a countable sum, allowing the model to be trained using standard methods like PyTorch.

open_questions.prompt: Explain the main idea of importance sampling for estimating likelihood to a classmate who missed the lecture.
open_questions.reference_answer: When estimating the likelihood of a data point $x$, naive Monte Carlo sampling is inefficient because most randomly sampled $z$'s will place nearly zero probability on $x$. Importance sampling solves this by changing the expectation to sample from a different density, $q(z)$. The goal is to choose $q(z)$ such that it gives more importance to the points that matter—specifically, the $z$'s that contribute high probability to $x$. The optimal distribution to sample from is $p(z|x)$, which allows us to get a good estimate with far fewer samples.
